lessons.title: Study Session 1: Projecting Cash Flow for the Weeks Ahead

blocks.text: Introduction Senait Fessehaye runs a small household goods shop in Barentu, and had always judged her cash position by what sat in the till on a given day, until a supplier payment fell due three weeks later than she had planned for, and even though her total revenue for the month was more than enough to cover it, the money simply was not there on the day the payment was needed. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about weekly cash flow budgeting for small businesses. Distinguish today's cash position from a projected future one. Apply a method for building a simple forward cash flow forecast. Recognise that a timing gap can exist even when total revenue is sufficient. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Enough Money, Wrong Week Senait Fessehaye's household goods shop in Barentu brought in enough revenue most months to cover every cost the business carried, including a large supplier payment due at the start of each quarter. Senait had never projected her cash position beyond the current day, and when the supplier payment fell due, the cash sitting in the shop that particular week fell well short of what was needed, even though the month's total revenue, once it had all come in, would have covered it several times over. 2.2 What Research Found About Weekly Cash Flow Budgeting Angela Busila reviewed strategies for seasonal small businesses managing cash flow for a 2025 paper, drawing on existing literature around cash budgeting and forecasting practice. Maintaining a weekly cash flow budget emerged as an effective, low-difficulty strategy for understanding a business's cash position ahead of time, giving owners information for decision making that a same-day view of the till could never provide. 2.3 Building a Forward Cash Flow Forecast Listing Known Inflows and Outflows by the Week They Fall Due Writing down every expected payment coming in and every expected payment going out against the specific week it is due, rather than against the month as a whole, shows exactly which week might fall short even when the wider month looks healthy. Carrying a Running Balance Forward Week by Week Starting each week's forecast with the balance left over from the week before, rather than resetting to zero, reveals a shortfall building up over several weeks before it actually arrives. 2.4 Key Practices List expected inflows and outflows against the specific week each one falls due. Carry the running balance forward from one week into the next. Update the forecast whenever a new payment date becomes known. Look several weeks ahead, not only at the current week's position. 2.5 A Worked Example: Senait's Four-Week Forecast Senait began listing every expected sale and every expected payment against the specific week each fell due, carrying her running cash balance forward from one week to the next rather than starting fresh each time. The forecast immediately showed a shortfall in the week the supplier payment was due, three weeks before that week actually arrived, giving Senait time to hold back a portion of earlier sales specifically to cover it. By the time the next quarterly payment came around, Senait's forecast had flagged the same kind of gap five weeks in advance, and the payment was made without any strain on the shop's daily cash. Senait's earlier habit of checking only the day's takings had not been careless. That habit simply stopped at today and was never designed to show what a specific future week would look like, and only a forecast carried forward week by week ever revealed that. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Judging cash health only by what sits in the till on a given day, without projecting forward to specific future weeks, means a business can be blindsided by a real payment even when its overall revenue is more than sufficient, exactly what happened to Senait. Forecasting only at the level of the month as a whole, rather than week by week, can hide a shortfall that sits inside one particular week even though the month's total looks fine. 2.7 Enough Money Overall Can Still Mean a Shortfall on One Day Senait's shop genuinely earned enough across a typical month to cover every cost it carried, including the supplier payment that once caught her by surprise. Earning enough overall had never guaranteed the money would be present on the specific day it was needed, and only a week-by-week forecast ever showed where that gap could open up. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a forward cash flow forecast that shows a timing gap before it happens. Study Session 2 turns from a general forward view to recognising a specific seasonal stretch where that gap is most likely to appear.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own cash position. Do you know what a specific week four weeks from now will look like, or only what today looks like? 2. Build a four-week forward cash flow forecast for one real business, listing expected inflows and outflows against the specific week each falls due. Practical Output: Practical Output A four-week forward cash flow forecast for one real business, with a running balance carried forward week by week. 7.0 References and Further Reading Busila, A. (2025). Thriving through seasonal cash flow challenges: Strategies for seasonal small businesses. Small Business Institute Journal, 21(2), 16 to 23. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Genesis 41:30, on years of famine arising after years of plenty. Qur'an, Surah Yunus 10:5, on the moon's phases determined so that the number of years and the reckoning of time might be known.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Spotting a Seasonal Cash Gap Before It Happens

blocks.text: Introduction Amina Boubacar is a single mother of two and keeps a grain and dried-produce stand at the Maradi market, trading heavily in the months after harvest and far more thinly in the months before the next one, and had always looked profitable across a full year on paper, until she noticed that the same few months kept leaving her short of cash no matter how strong the harvest season before them had been. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about small business seasonality and its phases. Distinguish a business that looks profitable over a year from one that has cash available in every month. Apply a method for planning specifically for a predictable seasonal trough. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Profitable for the Year, Short Every Same Few Months Amina Boubacar's produce stall in Maradi did strong trade for several months after each harvest and far less in the months leading up to the next one, a pattern that repeated every year. Looking at her full-year totals, the business appeared solidly profitable, yet Amina noticed that the same handful of months before each new harvest consistently left her short of cash, regardless of how well the previous busy season had gone. 2.2 What Research Found About Small Business Seasonality James Shields and Jaclyn Shelleman surveyed 73 small business owners for a 2013 study examining the cyclical demand patterns of seasonal businesses. Four distinct seasonal phases emerged from the research, a busy phase, a shouldering down phase, a slow phase and a shouldering up phase, each lasting one to three and a half months depending on the type of business, with owners managing cash very differently across each one. 2.3 Planning for a Predictable Seasonal Trough Naming the Specific Months a Trough Tends to Fall In Looking back over two or three years of records to identify the specific months where cash consistently runs thin, rather than treating each slow stretch as a surprise, turns a recurring pattern into something that can be planned around. Setting Aside a Specific Amount During the Busy Phase for the Trough Deciding, while cash is plentiful during a busy season, exactly how much needs to be set aside to carry the business through the identified trough months keeps that saving deliberate rather than whatever happens to be left over. 2.4 Key Practices Review two or three years of records to name the specific months a trough tends to fall in. Set aside a specific amount during the busy phase earmarked for the trough months. Treat the seasonal trough as an expected event to plan for, not a surprise to react to. Adjust spending and stock purchases ahead of the identified slow months. 2.5 A Worked Example: Amina's Named Trough Months Amina went back through three years of sales records and confirmed that the six weeks before each new harvest were consistently her thinnest period, regardless of how strong trading had been beforehand. She began setting aside a fixed portion of her busy-season income specifically earmarked for those six weeks, rather than letting whatever remained at the end of the busy season simply carry forward unplanned. The following pre-harvest trough passed without Amina needing to delay a single payment or draw down her children's school savings, the first time in years that stretch had not forced a difficult choice. Amina's earlier full-year profitability had never been an illusion, only an incomplete picture, silent on which specific months inside that year would be tight, and only naming the trough directly ever let her prepare for it on purpose. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Looking only at whether a business is profitable across a full year, without identifying which specific months tend to run short, allows the same seasonal trough to catch an owner off guard year after year, exactly what happened to Amina before she named her trough months directly. Treating a slow season as an unpredictable surprise, rather than an expected and repeating pattern, wastes the planning advantage a business actually has. 2.7 A Good Year Can Still Contain a Bad Stretch Amina's yearly totals had genuinely shown a profitable business for as long as she had been trading. That yearly total had never revealed which specific months inside it ran short, and only breaking the year down into its actual seasonal phases ever showed where the trouble consistently sat. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to name a predictable seasonal trough and plan for it in advance. Study Session 3 turns from a known, recurring seasonal pattern to preparing for a shock that cannot be predicted with the same certainty.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own business's trading pattern. Are there specific months that consistently run tighter than others? 2. Review two or three years of real records to name the specific months a seasonal trough tends to fall in, and set aside a specific amount for it. Practical Output: Practical Output A seasonal trough analysis for one real business, naming the specific months a slow stretch tends to fall in and a specific amount earmarked to cover it. 7.0 References and Further Reading Shields, J., & Shelleman, J. (2013). Small business seasonality: Characteristics and management. Small Business Institute Journal, 9(1), 37 to 50. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 6:8, on the ant providing her food in the summer and gathering it in the harvest. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:266, on a garden struck by a fiery whirlwind just when its owner was old and had weak children to provide for.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Stress-Testing a Forecast Against a Shock

blocks.text: Introduction Domingos Capenda supplies hardware and building materials to construction sites around Huambo, and had built a single cash forecast every quarter assuming deliveries would continue at a steady pace, until the main access road to several of his regular sites was closed for repairs for six weeks and his revenue dropped sharply with no alternative plan in place to fall back on. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about strategic foresight and financial resilience in SMEs. Distinguish a single steady-state forecast from a forecast tested against more than one scenario. Apply a method for building best-case, base-case and worst-case forecasts. Recognise the value of a tested plan when a shock actually occurs. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 One Forecast, One Version of the Future Domingos Capenda's hardware supply business in Huambo had, every quarter, built a single cash forecast assuming deliveries would continue at their usual steady pace. When the main access road to several of his regular construction sites closed for repairs for six weeks, deliveries and revenue dropped sharply, and Domingos had no alternative plan already prepared, having only ever forecast for the one version of the future where conditions stayed the same. 2.2 What Research Found About Strategic Foresight and Resilience Nomkhosi Radebe and colleagues surveyed 310 participants across mining sector SMEs in South Africa's Eastern Limb for a 2025 study, examining how strategic foresight practices related to financial performance and resilience. Scenario planning showed a substantial and favourable correlation with financial success, with SMEs that engaged in it found to be more adept at risk mitigation and at maintaining financial growth through periods of market uncertainty. 2.3 Building Best-Case, Base-Case and Worst-Case Forecasts Starting From a Base-Case Forecast Built on Current Trends Building one forecast on the assumption that recent trends and conditions continue roughly as they are gives a reasonable starting point before any adjustment for better or worse conditions is made. Adjusting That Base Case for a Plausible Better and Worse Scenario Taking the base-case forecast and adjusting its key assumptions, sales volume, a major cost, or access to customers, for one plausible better outcome and one plausible worse one produces a small set of forecasts ready before either actually happens. 2.4 Key Practices Build a base-case forecast from current trends before adjusting it in either direction. Adjust the base case for one plausible worse scenario and one plausible better one. Identify in advance what action each scenario would trigger. Revisit all three forecasts whenever a real shock or shift actually occurs. 2.5 A Worked Example: Domingos's Three Forecasts After the road closure, Domingos built a base-case forecast assuming normal delivery conditions, a worst-case forecast assuming a similar closure on his main route for up to two months, and a best-case forecast assuming an additional site came online. For the worst case, Domingos identified in advance which suppliers offered the most flexible payment terms and which non-essential costs could be paused immediately. When a second, shorter closure affected a different route eight months later, Domingos moved straight to his already-prepared worst-case actions rather than scrambling to work out a response from scratch, and the business absorbed the disruption with far less strain than the first closure had caused. Domingos's original single forecast had not been a careless one to build. It had simply only ever described one version of the future, and only preparing alternative versions in advance ever gave him something ready to reach for when conditions actually shifted. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building only a single forecast that assumes steady, unchanging conditions leaves a business with no prepared response when a real shock occurs, exactly the position Domingos found himself in during the first road closure. Waiting until a shock has already happened to think through a response, rather than preparing scenarios in advance, wastes valuable time exactly when a fast response matters most. 2.7 A Single Forecast Only Describes a Single Future Domingos's original forecast had genuinely reflected the business's normal, steady conditions accurately for as long as those conditions held. Accuracy under normal conditions had never meant the forecast would hold once conditions changed, and only building alternative versions in advance ever left Domingos with a plan ready for the version that actually arrived. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build best-case, base-case and worst-case forecasts rather than a single steady-state one. Study Session 4 turns from preparing for what might happen to checking what actually did happen against the budget already in place.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own forecasting habits. Have you ever prepared more than one version of a forecast for different conditions? 2. Build a base-case, worst-case and best-case forecast for one real business, identifying what action each scenario would trigger. Practical Output: Practical Output Three versions of a cash flow forecast, base-case, worst-case and best-case, for one real business, each with a pre-identified response. 7.0 References and Further Reading Radebe, N., Sefora, R., Nemaduvhetshewe, C.N., & Karbelkar, M. (2025). From strategy to success: The path to financial resilience through strategic foresight in mining SMEs. International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy, 7(3), 1 to 17. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Matthew 7:25, on the rain descending, the floods coming and the winds blowing upon a house founded on rock, and it not falling. Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12:43, on the king asking for an interpretation of seven fat cows and seven lean ones.

quiz.q: Senait's shop had enough monthly revenue to cover a supplier payment, yet still fell short the week it was due. What did this reveal?
options: Senait's shop had genuinely been unprofitable that quarter
Sufficient revenue across a month does not guarantee enough cash is present in the specific week a payment falls due
Household goods shops should not accept supplier credit terms
Senait had miscounted her daily takings
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Projecting Cash Flow for the Weeks Ahead) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Busila's 2025 research, what did maintaining a weekly cash flow budget provide for small business owners?
options: No additional information beyond a same-day view of the till
Information for decision making that a same-day view could not provide
A guarantee that no future shortfall could ever occur
A replacement for tracking daily cash entirely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Projecting Cash Flow for the Weeks Ahead) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing with each week's forecast balance?
options: Resetting it to zero at the start of every week
Carrying it forward from the previous week
Ignoring it unless a payment is already overdue
Recalculating it only once a year
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Projecting Cash Flow for the Weeks Ahead) before continuing.

quiz.q: Amina's business looked profitable across the full year, yet the same months consistently left her short of cash. What did this reveal?
options: Amina's harvest-season sales had been recorded incorrectly
A business can look profitable across a full year while still containing specific months that consistently run short
Seasonal produce businesses should not be operated in Maradi
Amina's customers had stopped buying from her entirely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Spotting a Seasonal Cash Gap Before It Happens) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Shields and Shelleman's 2013 study, how many distinct seasonal phases did they identify?
options: Two phases, busy and slow
Four phases: busy, shouldering down, slow, and shouldering up
Six phases corresponding to each two-month stretch
One continuous phase with no real variation
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Spotting a Seasonal Cash Gap Before It Happens) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing during a business's busy phase?
options: Spending all available cash immediately
Setting aside a specific amount earmarked for the identified trough months
Ignoring the trough until it actually arrives
Reducing prices to attract more customers
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Spotting a Seasonal Cash Gap Before It Happens) before continuing.

modules.title: Part 2
modules.overview: Cash-Flow and Business Budgeting — Part 2. Study each session, complete the reflection and practical output, and pass the part quiz before moving forward.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Comparing Actual Results Against the Budget

blocks.text: Introduction Aminata Zongo caters weddings and naming ceremonies for clients across Dedougou and had built a proper budget at the start of the year, listing expected income and costs in detail, but never once set her actual monthly results beside that budget to check them, until she finally compared the two at year's end and found the gap between what she had planned and what had actually happened had grown far larger than she expected. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about budget planning and SME financial performance. Distinguish a budget that is regularly checked against actual results from one left unexamined. Apply a method for comparing actual results against a budget on a regular rhythm. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Budget Built Once and Never Checked Aminata Zongo's catering business had a proper budget built at the start of the year, with income and costs laid out in real detail. Aminata never returned to that budget during the year to check it against her bookings, and when she finally sat down at year's end to look at both together, several categories had drifted far further from the original plan than she had realised, in ways that could have been caught and corrected months earlier. 2.2 What Research Found About Budget Planning and SME Performance Jepleting Gladys, John Tarus and Zachariah Shitote surveyed small and medium enterprises in Eldoret Town, Kenya, for a 2024 study, examining how budget planning practices related to financial performance. Budget planning was found to have a significant effect on financial performance among the enterprises studied, an effect further strengthened where digital finance services supported the ongoing comparison of actual figures against the plan. 2.3 Comparing Actual Results Against a Budget Regularly Setting a Fixed Point Each Month to Compare the Two Choosing a specific day each month to place actual income and cost figures directly beside the budgeted ones turns a comparison that could easily be postponed into a fixed habit that actually happens. Recording the Gap in Each Category, Not Only the Overall Total Checking every individual budget category against its actual figure, not just the grand total at the bottom of the page, catches a category that has drifted even when the totals happen to look close. 2.4 Key Practices Set a fixed monthly day to compare actual figures against the budget. Check every individual category, not only the overall totals. Note the size of the gap in each category, whether favourable or unfavourable. Treat a growing gap as worth attention immediately, not at year's end. 2.5 A Worked Example: Aminata's Monthly Comparison Aminata set the last day of every month as her fixed point to place actual income and costs beside her original budget, category by category, rather than waiting for the year to end. The very first comparison showed that her ingredient costs were already running noticeably above budget, a gap that had been invisible in the overall monthly total because stronger-than-expected catering bookings had been quietly covering it. Catching that gap in its first month let Aminata renegotiate with a supplier before the difference grew any larger, something that would have been far harder to unwind by year's end. Aminata's original budget had not been a poorly built one, but it went untested against reality from the day it was written until she began her monthly comparisons, and only that regular check ever showed where the two had begun to pull apart. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building a detailed budget and then never comparing it against actual results during the year means a gap can grow for months before anyone notices it, exactly what happened to Aminata before she began checking monthly. Checking only the two grand totals against each other, instead of every category on its own, can hide a real gap sitting inside one category while other categories happen to offset it. 2.7 A Budget Left Unchecked Is Still Just a Document Aminata's original budget had genuinely been built with care, its figures grounded in real expected income and costs. Care at the drafting stage said nothing about what would happen to the business afterward, and only setting actual results beside the budget regularly ever turned it into something that could still guide a decision partway through the year. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to compare actual results against a budget on a regular monthly rhythm. Study Session 5 turns from noticing that a gap exists to tracing a persistent one back to what actually caused it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about a budget you have built. Has it ever been compared against actual results before the end of the period it covers? 2. Compare one real month's actual income and costs against a budget, category by category, and note the size of each gap. Practical Output: Practical Output A category-by-category comparison of one real month's actual results against a budget, with the size of each gap recorded. 7.0 References and Further Reading Gladys, J., Tarus, J., & Shitote, Z. (2024). Effects of budget planning on financial performance of selected SMEs in Eldoret Town, Kenya, moderated by digital finance services. International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science, 8(11), 716 to 729. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 12:48, on much being required of the one to whom much has been given. Qur'an, Surah At-Takathur 102:8, on being asked, on that Day, about the pleasure enjoyed.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Investigating Why a Variance Happened

blocks.text: Introduction Fadimata Wallet fled fighting in her home region and now sews and trades cloth from a stall she built up piece by piece in Kidal, and had learned to compare her monthly figures against her budget, but for months simply logged a persistent unfavourable gap in her fabric costs without asking why it existed, until she finally dug into the figures and traced it back to a supplier who had quietly raised one specific input's price many months earlier. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about variance analysis and SME financial performance. Distinguish noting a variance from investigating its actual cause. Apply a method for tracing a persistent variance back to its root cause. Recognise the specific kinds of hidden causes a variance investigation tends to uncover. Apply variance investigation to correct a real budget assumption. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Gap Noted Every Month, Understood by None Fadimata Wallet's tailoring and textile trading business in Kidal had, for several months running, shown a persistent unfavourable gap between budgeted and actual fabric costs. Fadimata recorded that gap faithfully each month as part of her routine comparison, but never went further to ask what was actually causing it, until she finally sat down and traced the figures back, discovering that one specific fabric supplier had quietly raised a key price many months before, a change Fadimata's original budget had never been updated to reflect. 2.2 What Research Found About Variance Analysis in SMEs Lordwin Paa Kwesi Archer surveyed 200 small and medium enterprises in Ghana for a 2026 study, examining four dimensions of budgetary control, formal budgets, review frequency, participative budgeting, and variance analysis, against financial performance. Variance analysis on its own did not significantly influence financial performance, while regular review and active engagement with a budget's figures did, a finding that pointed to noting a variance being of little value unless it was actually investigated and acted upon. 2.3 Tracing a Variance Back to Its Root Cause Asking What Specifically Changed Behind a Persistent Gap Breaking a category showing a persistent variance down into its individual components, a specific supplier, a specific input, a specific rate, rather than treating the whole category as one figure, is what actually surfaces which single change is driving the gap. Checking the Date a Suspected Cause Actually Began Tracing back through past records to find the exact point a suspected cause first appeared confirms whether it genuinely explains the variance or is simply a coincidence sitting alongside it. 2.4 Key Practices Break a persistent variance down into its individual components rather than treating it as one figure. Ask what specifically changed behind the gap, not only that a gap exists. Check the exact date a suspected cause began to confirm it actually explains the variance. Update the budget assumption once the real cause has been confirmed. 2.5 A Worked Example: Fadimata's Fabric Cost Investigation Fadimata went back through her fabric purchase records line by line and found that one particular cotton blend, used in roughly a third of her orders, had risen in price several months before the variance first appeared in her monthly comparisons, while every other fabric she bought had stayed close to budget the entire time. Once she confirmed the timing matched exactly, Fadimata updated her budget to reflect the new price and adjusted the prices of the garments that used that specific fabric. The following month's comparison showed the fabric cost variance had closed almost entirely, and Fadimata began checking the timing of any new variance immediately rather than letting it sit unexplained for months as the fabric cost gap once had. Noting the gap every month had never, by itself, been a wasted habit for Fadimata. It had simply stopped short of the one step that actually mattered, and only tracing the gap back to its specific cause ever gave her something she could act on. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Noting that a variance exists month after month, without ever investigating what is actually causing it, leaves a business repeating the same unexplained gap indefinitely, exactly what happened to Fadimata before she traced her fabric costs. Treating a whole budget category as one figure, rather than breaking it down into its individual components, makes it far harder to find the single change actually driving a persistent gap. 2.7 Noticing a Gap Is Only the First Step Fadimata had genuinely noticed her fabric cost variance every single month for a considerable stretch of time, faithfully recording it each time. That faithful noticing had never, by itself, told her what was actually behind the gap, and only breaking the category down and checking dates directly ever traced it back to the one supplier's price change responsible. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to trace a persistent variance back to its specific root cause rather than only noting that it exists. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a forecast is kept current through continual revision rather than treated as fixed for the year.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about a variance you have noticed in your own budget. Have you ever traced it back to its specific cause, or only recorded that it exists? 2. Investigate one real persistent variance by breaking it into its components and checking when the likely cause actually began. Practical Output: Practical Output A variance investigation for one real budget category, tracing the gap to its specific cause and updating the budget assumption accordingly. 7.0 References and Further Reading Archer, L.P.K. (2026). The impact of budgetary control on financial performance: Evidence from SMEs in Ghana. Global Journal of Management and Business Research, 25(A6), 35 to 43. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 18:15, on the heart of the prudent getting knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeking it out. Qur'an, Surah Az-Zalzalah 99:8, on whoever does an atom's weight of evil seeing it.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Rolling the Forecast Forward

blocks.text: Introduction Eric Habimana runs a small welding and repair workshop in Muhanga, and had always treated his annual budget as a document to be built once at the start of the year and left alone until the next one, so that by the time October arrived, the figures he was still working from no longer reflected a single month of what had actually happened since March. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about rolling budgets and business uncertainty. Distinguish a fixed annual budget from a forecast that rolls forward continually. Apply a method for updating a forecast on a regular cycle using the latest actuals. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Budget Frozen in March, Still in Use in October Eric Habimana's welding and repair workshop in Muhanga had, every year, built a detailed budget in March and then left it untouched until the following year's budget was built. By October, the workshop's actual trading looked considerably different from what the March figures had assumed, new customers gained, one supplier lost, material costs shifted, yet Eric was still comparing that month's results against numbers that had not been updated in seven months. 2.2 What Research Found About Rolling Budgets and Uncertainty Alnoor Bhimani, Prabhu Sivabalan and Kimberly Soonawalla examined how rolling budgets related to uncertainty and strategy for a 2018 study, drawing on responses from 182 firms already using some form of rolling budget. Monthly rolling budgets showed a far greater sensitivity to shifts in uncertainty and strategy than budgets updated only quarterly, suggesting that how often a forecast is rolled forward matters as much as whether it is rolled forward at all. 2.3 Updating a Forecast on a Regular Cycle Adding a Fresh Period Onto the End Each Time One Closes Extending the forecast by one new period, whether a month or a quarter, each time the current one closes keeps a business always looking the same distance ahead, rather than looking progressively less far forward as a fixed annual budget ages. Feeding the Latest Actuals and Variance Findings Back Into the Forecast Carrying forward what a recent variance investigation actually revealed, and adjusting the forecast's assumptions accordingly, keeps the forecast reflecting the business as it currently operates rather than as it operated when the original budget was first written. 2.4 Key Practices Add a fresh period onto the forecast each time the current one closes. Feed the latest actual figures and confirmed variance causes back into the forecast's assumptions. Set a fixed monthly or quarterly point to roll the forecast forward. Retire assumptions that no longer match how the business currently operates. 2.5 A Worked Example: Eric's Rolling Monthly Forecast Eric moved from a single annual budget to a forecast that extended one further month every time the current month closed, updating its assumptions each time with the latest actual figures and any variance causes he had confirmed that month. By the following March, Eric's forecast reflected the new customers he had gained, the supplier he had lost, and the material cost shift, all folded in gradually rather than discovered all at once a year later. The workshop's decisions through the following year, including a decision to take on a second welder, were made against figures that were at most a few weeks old rather than nearly a year stale. Eric's original annual budget had been sound when he first drafted it, yet it sat unrevised while the workshop itself kept changing around it, and only rolling it forward continually ever kept the two moving together. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building a budget once a year and leaving it unchanged until the next annual cycle means decisions late in the year are made against figures that no longer reflect how the business actually operates, exactly what happened to Eric before he began rolling his forecast forward. Rolling a forecast forward only occasionally, rather than on a fixed and frequent cycle, weakens its sensitivity to real shifts in the business, precisely the gap the research found between monthly and quarterly rolling budgets. 2.7 A Forecast Stops Being Useful the Moment It Stops Moving Eric's original March budget had genuinely reflected the workshop's situation accurately on the day it was written. That accuracy at a single point in time had never meant it would still describe the business seven months later, and only rolling the forecast forward continually ever kept it describing the workshop as it actually was. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to roll a forecast forward on a regular cycle rather than treating it as fixed for the year. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Supplier Negotiation Basics for Small Enterprises, the next course in Pathway 58.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own budget. Is it still describing your business as it currently operates, or as it operated when it was first written? 2. Roll one real forecast forward by a further period, updating its assumptions with the latest actual figures and any confirmed variance causes. Practical Output: Practical Output A rolled-forward forecast for one real business, extended by a further period and updated with the latest actual figures and confirmed variance causes. 7.0 References and Further Reading Bhimani, A., Sivabalan, P., & Soonawalla, K.
